659.title: The Chrism Mass
659.hook: the bishop blesses the oils for the whole year's sacraments
659.howItsDone: At the Chrism Mass in Holy Week, the bishop blesses the oil of catechumens and the oil of the sick and consecrates the sacred chrism, and the priests of the diocese renew their ordination promises; each parish then receives the oils for the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Palm Sunday: hosanna at the door, crucify in the Passion. Your line was hosanna, then crucify.

In a Catholic parish church, often near the font or in a small cabinet in the wall called an ambry, there are three little vessels of oil. Every baby baptized there this year, every teenager confirmed, every elderly person anointed in a hospital bed, will be touched with oil from those vessels. And all of it came from one Mass, in one cathedral, during Holy Week, when the bishop and the priests of the diocese gathered in the same place.
screen: `THREE SMALL VESSELS.` → `EVERY BAPTISM, EVERY ANOINTING.` → `ONE MASS, ONE CATHEDRAL.`

segments.voice: It's called the Chrism Mass, traditionally celebrated on the morning of Holy Thursday, though some dioceses hold it earlier in Holy Week so priests from far-off parishes can come. Jars of olive oil are carried up the aisle, and the bishop blesses three. The oil of catechumens, for people preparing for baptism: a sign of strength for the struggle ahead. The oil of the sick, for the anointing of the sick. The letter of James describes it: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." And the third, the sacred chrism. It's olive oil mixed with balsam, a fragrant resin, so it smells sweet. The bishop consecrates it, and by an old custom he breathes over it, a sign of the Spirit. Chrism is used at baptism, at confirmation, at the ordination of priests and bishops, and to consecrate altars and churches. Christ is a Greek title meaning anointed one; John's Gospel says so outright, that Messias, being interpreted, is the Christ. So chrism and Christ share a root. To be anointed with it is to be marked as belonging to the anointed one. The gospel at this Mass is Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth, reading from Isaiah: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." Then the priests stand and renew the promises they made at ordination. The oils go home to every parish, oil for the whole year.

segments.voice: Catholics are asked to pray for their priests at this Mass, so if you pray, hold yours in mind: your pastor, the priest who baptized you, one who buried someone you loved. If you're not Catholic, think of anyone who cared for you in a hard moment, a chaplain, a nurse, a friend, and picture their hands. Wish them strength for their own hard days.

660.title: Holy Thursday
660.hook: the washing of feet, the new commandment, and the watch at the altar of repose
660.howItsDone: At the Evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, the priest may wash the feet of members of the congregation, the Eucharist is carried to an altar of repose, the main altar is stripped, and the faithful keep watch, often until midnight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the holy oils, blessed at the Chrism Mass and sent to every parish. Your line was oil for the whole year.

In English the day is sometimes called Maundy Thursday, an odd word that hides its meaning. In Britain the monarch gives out special coins that day. In parish churches something stranger happens: after the homily, the priest takes off his outer vestment, ties a towel around his waist, kneels on the floor, and washes the feet of people chosen from the congregation. The odd English word and the odd ritual come from the same Latin word.
screen: `MAUNDY THURSDAY.` → `A TOWEL AROUND THE WAIST.` → `ONE LATIN WORD.`

segments.voice: Holy Thursday evening begins the Triduum, the three great days. The Mass of the Lord's Supper remembers the night Jesus gave his disciples the Eucharist, and the gospel is John 13. During supper, Jesus gets up, lays aside his garments, takes a towel, pours water into a basin, and washes his disciples' feet, a job usually left to servants. Peter protests: you will never wash my feet. Jesus says, if I don't wash you, you have no part with me. Then he sits back down and explains: if I, your Lord and master, have washed your feet, you ought to wash one another's. And a little later, the command: "A new commandment I give unto you: That you love one another, as I have loved you." In Latin, commandment is mandatum, and from mandatum comes maundy. So the rite of foot washing is called the Mandatum. The Gloria is sung tonight with the bells ringing, and then the bells fall silent until the Easter Vigil. After communion, the remaining consecrated hosts are carried in procession to a side altar, the altar of repose, decked with flowers and candles. The main altar is stripped bare. And people stay. They keep watch, often until midnight, remembering Gethsemane, where Jesus asked his friends to stay awake while he prayed in anguish, and found them sleeping. In the Douay-Rheims: "What? Could you not watch one hour with me?" On this night, some Catholics walk from church to church, visiting several altars of repose, keeping company with him in each.
screen: `THE TRIDUUM BEGINS.` · `A TOWEL AND A BASIN.` · `MANDATUM: THE NEW COMMANDMENT.` · `THE WATCH AT THE ALTAR OF REPOSE.` · then, large: `LOVE ONE ANOTHER, AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.`

segments.voice: On this night people keep watch at the altar of repose, and an hour is the old measure; for now, sit wherever you are and keep company. Picture the garden, olive trees, the dark, friends asleep, one man praying, and stay awake with him. If you pray, simply stay, no words needed; if you don't, keep watch for someone you know who is suffering tonight.

661.title: Good Friday
661.hook: John's passion, prayers for the whole world, and the veneration of the cross
661.carry: behold the wood of the cross
661.howItsDone: On Good Friday Catholics celebrate the Passion of the Lord, often at 3 p.m., with John's Passion, the Solemn Intercessions, the veneration of the cross and Communion; no Mass is celebrated, and it is a day of fasting and abstinence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandatum: a towel, a basin, and the new commandment. Your line was love one another.

Three o'clock on a Friday afternoon. People in the pews, and almost no sound. The altar is bare. No bells, no opening song. The priest and ministers walk in without a word, and then the priest does something you won't see on an ordinary Sunday: he lies face down on the floor, or kneels, and stays there in silence. Nobody explains it. Everyone waits. Today, in the Roman Rite, there is no Mass at all.
screen: `THREE O'CLOCK, ALMOST NO SOUND.` → `FACE DOWN ON THE FLOOR.` → `NO MASS TODAY.`

segments.voice: The service, often at three in the afternoon, the hour Jesus died, has three parts. First, the readings: Isaiah's suffering servant, wounded for our iniquities, and then, every year, the Passion from John's gospel, often read in parts. John's Jesus is strikingly calm. In the garden, when the soldiers come, he steps forward and says, I am he, and they fall back. He carries his own cross. From it he gives his mother and his beloved disciple to each other. And his last words, in the Douay-Rheims, are: "It is consummated." Finished, completed, the work done. Then the second part, the Solemn Intercessions: ten long prayers for the whole world. For the Church and the pope, for those preparing for baptism, for Christian unity, for the Jewish people, for those who don't believe in Christ or in God, for leaders, and for everyone who suffers. Nobody is left out. Then the third part. A cross is carried up the aisle, unveiled in stages or carried in procession, and the priest sings in the old Latin: "Ecce lignum Crucis." Behold the wood of the cross, on which hung the salvation of the world. Come, let us adore. And people come forward one by one to genuflect, touch, or kiss the wood. Communion follows, from hosts consecrated the night before, and everyone leaves in silence. Catholics fast today. And why call it good? Some say the word once carried a sense close to holy. Catholics call it good because of what they believe was finished on the cross.
screen: `JOHN'S PASSION: I AM HE.` · `IT IS CONSUMMATED.` · `TEN PRAYERS FOR THE WORLD.` · `ECCE LIGNUM CRUCIS.` · then, large: `BEHOLD THE WOOD OF THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: If there's a crucifix in your home, a cross on a chain, or one in a church you can reach, hold it, touch it or kiss it the way people do at the veneration; if you have none, trace one on your palm with a finger. Then sit in silence, the way the church does today, and let it be heavy if it's heavy. If you pray, whisper the old words, behold the wood of the cross; if you don't, simply stay with the silence.
Good Friday. The day of the Lord's Passion: no Mass, John's Passion, prayers for the whole world, and the veneration of the cross. Today's word.
Your line: behold the wood of the cross. The quiet holds until the Vigil. See you tomorrow.

662.title: Holy Saturday
662.hook: the tabernacle open and empty, the church stripped
662.howItsDone: On Holy Saturday Catholic churches keep the altar bare and the tabernacle empty, no Mass is celebrated during the day, and many Catholics fast, pray quietly, or visit the church before the Easter Vigil after nightfall.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Good Friday, and the cross carried up the aisle. Your line was behold the wood of the cross.

Holy Thursday has a supper. Good Friday has a cross. Easter has an empty tomb. In between sits a whole day with almost nothing on it. No Mass from morning until nightfall. The tabernacle stands open and empty, as it was left yesterday, and in many parishes the holy water fonts by the door are dry. Somebody might be arranging lilies in a side room for tonight, but out in the church, nothing happens. On purpose.
screen: `THURSDAY, FRIDAY, SUNDAY.` → `A DAY WITH ALMOST NOTHING ON IT.` → `NO MASS UNTIL NIGHTFALL.`

segments.voice: The Gospels say very little about this day, and that silence is the point. Matthew tells us the authorities sealed the stone and set guards. Luke gives one plain sentence about the women who had watched the burial, in the Douay-Rheims: "And on the sabbath day they rested, according to the commandment." The women who loved him most spent the day keeping the sabbath, with spices waiting in a jar for Sunday morning. They were not waiting for a resurrection. They were waiting to anoint a body. So the Church keeps the day the way they did: nothing added. The Missal says the Church waits at the Lord's tomb, praying and fasting, and the altar stays bare. The empty tabernacle is the loudest sign of all. The consecrated hosts were moved from the main altar on Thursday night, given out at Friday's service, and any left over taken to a quiet place apart; Christ's presence, in the way Catholics speak of it, is not kept in the church today. But Catholics don't say the day is empty of him. The Apostles' Creed says he descended into hell, and Catholic teaching is that he went down among the dead, to the righteous who had waited since Adam, to bring them out. An ancient homily for this day, read in the Church's Office of Readings, pictures him taking Adam by the hand. On earth, a great silence. Underneath it, something is happening that nobody can see yet. That's the shape of a lot of real waiting: a hospital corridor, an inbox, a hard year. Holy Saturday gives that feeling a place in the calendar, and doesn't rush it.
screen: `THE GOSPELS SAY ALMOST NOTHING.` · `THE WOMEN RESTED, SPICES READY.` · `THE CHURCH WAITS AT THE TOMB.` · `HE DESCENDED AMONG THE DEAD.` · then, large: `AND ON THE SABBATH DAY THEY RESTED.`

segments.voice: Sit somewhere still with your phone face down: near the open tabernacle if you can reach a church, or a parked car, a bench, the edge of your bed. Think of one thing in your life you're still waiting on, and let it stay unresolved for a while, without praying or planning. If you pray, you can simply stay, the way the women stayed.

663.title: The Easter Vigil readings
663.hook: up to seven readings, from creation to Ezekiel, before the alleluia
663.carry: the whole story in one night
663.howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, Catholics gather after dark, light the Easter candle from a new fire, hear up to seven Old Testament readings with psalms, then sing the Gloria and the first alleluia since Lent; adults preparing for baptism are baptized and confirmed at this Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holy Saturday: the bare altar, the open tabernacle. Your line was the day of waiting.

It's dark outside, and the church is dark inside. A fire is lit at the door. A single tall candle is carried in, and the flame passes hand to hand down the pews until the whole room is lit by small candles. A deacon or cantor sings the Exsultet, the great Easter proclamation. Then everyone sits down, because this is going to take a while. Before anyone says alleluia, the Church opens the Bible at page one and reads its way forward.
screen: `A FIRE AT THE DOOR.` → `ONE CANDLE, THEN HUNDREDS.` → `BACK TO PAGE ONE.`

segments.voice: The Missal gives seven readings from the Old Testament, each followed by a psalm and a prayer. It starts with creation, in the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning God created heaven, and earth." And soon: "Be light made. And light was made." In that church, the candle that just came in the door was the first light, too. Then Abraham on the mountain with Isaac. Then the sea parting at the Exodus, the one reading the Missal says may never be left out, because that crossing from slavery to freedom is the pattern for Easter. Then the prophets: Isaiah promising a love that won't leave, and water and bread for anyone who's thirsty; Baruch praising wisdom; and last, Ezekiel, where God promises to take away the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh. Parishes may shorten the list, but the Missal asks for at least three, and the Red Sea always stays. Then the candles on the altar are lit, the bells ring out for the Gloria, and the reading from Romans says that in baptism we are buried with Christ and rise with him. Only then does the alleluia return, sung for the first time since Lent began. Why read the whole story? Because the Church's claim is that Easter isn't a lucky ending tacked on. It's what the whole story was heading toward, from the first light. Adults preparing for baptism are baptized at this Mass, after the readings and the homily. They hear the family history on the night they join the family.
screen: `IT BEGINS WITH CREATION.` · `THE RED SEA NEVER SKIPPED.` · `A HEART OF STONE, A HEART OF FLESH.` · `THEN THE BELLS, THEN THE ALLELUIA.` · then, large: `BE LIGHT MADE. AND LIGHT WAS MADE.`

664.title: Easter Sunday
664.hook: the tomb is empty and the alleluia returns
664.howItsDone: On Easter Sunday Catholics celebrate Mass with the Gospel of the empty tomb, sing the alleluia that was silent through Lent, end Mass with a double alleluia, and often greet each other with Christ is risen and the answer he is risen indeed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Exsultet, and the whole Bible story read by candlelight. Your line was the whole story in one night.

Since Ash Wednesday, a single word has been missing from the Mass. Not dropped by accident: put away. In some places, children even wrote it on a banner before Lent and buried it in the churchyard. All through Lent the Gospel was greeted with other words. Then last night, after the readings, the priest sang it three times, each time a little higher, and the people sang it back. This morning it's everywhere: on the doors, in the hymns, doubled at the end of Mass.
screen: `ALL LENT WITHOUT IT.` → `SUNG THREE TIMES, RISING.` → `EASTER MORNING.`

segments.voice: Start with the morning Gospel. On Easter Sunday the Church reads John. Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb while it's still dark and finds the stone rolled away. She runs to Peter and the other disciple, the one Jesus loved, and the two of them race back. The other disciple outruns Peter, gets there first, looks in, and waits. Peter goes straight in and sees the linen cloths lying there, and the face cloth rolled up by itself. Then the other disciple goes in, and John says he saw and believed. No angel's speech, no appearance yet. Just two out-of-breath men and an empty room. Matthew puts it in an angel's mouth, in the Douay-Rheims: "He is not here, for he is risen, as he said." Now the word. Alleluia is Hebrew: hallelu, praise, plural, all of you, and Yah, the short form of God's name. Praise the Lord, everybody. It opens and closes a run of Psalms, and the Book of Revelation has heaven singing it. The Church buried it for Lent so that it could come back like this. Today the dismissal at the end of Mass gets a double alleluia, and it will keep it through the eight days of the octave and again at Pentecost. Some Catholics also use a greeting from the Christian East this morning: one person says Christ is risen, and the other answers, he is risen indeed. Christians say the tomb was empty because he was raised, and Paul writes that if Christ is not risen, their preaching is in vain. A great deal rests on that empty room.

665.title: The Easter Octave
665.hook: eight days counted as one great day
665.howItsDone: During the Easter octave Catholics celebrate each day from Easter Sunday to the following Sunday as a solemnity, with the Gloria at Mass and a double alleluia at the dismissal; in many countries Easter Monday is a public holiday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter Sunday and the word that came back. Your line was alleluia.

Most parties end when the guests go home. By Tuesday it's just Tuesday. The Church does something odd with Easter. On Monday the Gloria is sung again. On Tuesday, again. All week the prayers at Mass keep saying this day, today, as if the sun hadn't set, and the dismissal still ends with a double alleluia. In parts of Europe, Easter Monday is a public holiday, and the visiting goes on. The calendar refuses to turn the page.
screen: `THE GLORIA ON MONDAY.` → `STILL SAYING THIS DAY.` → `THE PAGE DOESN'T TURN.`

segments.voice: An octave comes from the Latin octava, the eighth. In the calendar, it means a feast kept for eight days, from the day itself to the same weekday a week later. The Church's rules say it plainly: the first eight days of the Easter season make up the octave of Easter and are celebrated as solemnities of the Lord. Every one of them outranks almost anything else. That's why, in the Church's daily prayer, the Liturgy of the Hours, the Easter line from the Psalm, This is the day which the Lord hath made, comes back at every hour all week. It isn't eight Easters. It's one great day stretched across eight. Why eight? Early Christians noticed that Jesus rose on the first day of the week, which is also the day after the seventh: the eighth day. The Epistle of Barnabas and Justin Martyr call Sunday the eighth day, the start of a new creation beyond the old week. Some old baptismal fonts have eight sides, and some readers see the same idea there. And tradition says the newly baptized from the Vigil wore their white garments through this week. The octave ends next Sunday. Only two octaves remain in the Roman calendar now, Christmas and Easter. And this closes week ninety-five: the oils blessed at the Chrism Mass, the washing of feet on Holy Thursday, the wood of the cross on Good Friday, the waiting of Holy Saturday, the whole story at the Vigil, the empty tomb, and now one long day.
